tasks.description: Write a generator function `count_up(n)` that yields numbers from 1 to n. Loop over it and print each value.
tasks.hint:
`yield` pauses the function and returns a value — the function resumes from that point next time.
`def count_up(n): for i in range(1, n+1): yield i`
Loop it like any iterable: `for num in count_up(5): print(num)`
tasks.walkthrough:
Each pass of the inner loop yields one number and pauses.
The outer `for` requests values one at a time until the generator finishes, so it prints 1 to 5.

tasks.description: Write a generator `squares()` that yields the squares of 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 indefinitely (or for 5 values). Use next() to get the first 3.
tasks.hint:
`def squares(): i = 1
  while True: yield i**2; i += 1` — infinite generator.
`gen = squares(); print(next(gen))` calls the generator manually.
`next()` gets the next value — call it 3 times.
tasks.solution:
def squares():
    i = 1
    while True:
        yield i ** 2
        i += 1

gen = squares()
print(next(gen))
print(next(gen))
print(next(gen))
tasks.walkthrough:
The `while True` never ends, but that's fine: the body only runs when a value is asked for.
Three calls to `next()` produce the first three squares and then the generator sits paused.

tasks.description: Write a generator `fibonacci()` that yields Fibonacci numbers (0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8...). Print the first 8.
tasks.hint:
Track two values: `a, b = 0, 1`
Each iteration: `yield a` then `a, b = b, a + b` — this updates both at once.
Use `for _, n in zip(range(8), fibonacci()): print(n)` or a loop with a counter.
tasks.walkthrough:
`a` is the current number and `b` is the next. After yielding `a`, both move along in one assignment.
`zip(range(8), ...)` stops after 8 pairs, which limits the infinite generator to 8 values.

tasks.description: Convert a generator expression `(x**2 for x in range(1, 6))` to a list and print it. Compare to a list comprehension.
tasks.hint:
`(expression for var in iterable)` creates a generator — note the `()` not `[]`.
Generators are LAZY — they don't compute values until needed.
`list(x**2 for x in range(1, 6))` forces all values to be computed now.
tasks.solution:
gen = (x ** 2 for x in range(1, 6))
print(list(gen))
tasks.walkthrough:
Round brackets make a generator expression; square brackets would make a list straight away.
`list(gen)` pulls every value out of the generator, giving exactly what `[x ** 2 for x in range(1, 6)]` would.
The difference is that the generator computed nothing until `list()` asked. Try printing `gen` on its own to see the generator object.

tasks.description: Write a generator `read_lines(text)` that takes a multi-line string and yields each line one at a time (stripped).
tasks.hint:
Split the text on `'\n'`: `for line in text.split('\n'): yield line.strip()`
Generators are memory-efficient for large data — they don't load everything at once.
Test with a 3-line string and loop the generator.
tasks.walkthrough:
The text is split on newlines and each piece is stripped of surrounding spaces before being yielded.
With a real file you'd loop over the file object instead of splitting a string, but the generator shape is the same.

lesson.intro:
A normal function runs, returns one value, and is done. A generator hands out
values one at a time and pauses in between, remembering where it was. That
makes it possible to work through huge or even endless sequences without
holding them all in memory.

sections.heading: yield instead of return
sections.body:
Any function with `yield` in it becomes a generator. Calling it doesn't run
the body; it gives you a generator object. Each time a value is requested,
the body runs until the next `yield`, hands that value out, and pauses.

sections.heading: Pulling values by hand with next()
sections.body:
`next(gen)` asks for one more value. When the generator runs out, `next`
raises StopIteration, which is how a `for` loop knows to stop.
sections.code:
def squares():
    i = 1
    while True:
        yield i ** 2
        i += 1

gen = squares()
print(next(gen))
print(next(gen))
print(next(gen))

sections.heading: Infinite sequences are fine
sections.body:
Because nothing is computed until asked for, a generator can go on forever.
You take what you need. Fibonacci is the classic example. `zip` with a
`range` is a tidy way to take the first n.

sections.heading: Generator expressions
sections.body:
A list comprehension with round brackets instead of square ones. It looks
the same but produces a generator: lazy, one value at a time. Pass it to
`list()`, `sum()`, `max()` or a loop.
sections.code:
gen = (x ** 2 for x in range(1, 6))
print(gen)
print(list(gen))
print(sum(x ** 2 for x in range(1, 6)))

watch_out: A generator can only be gone through once. After it's exhausted, looping again gives nothing.
Printing a generator object shows its address, not its values. Convert with `list()` if you want to see them.
`return` inside a generator ends it. Values after that are never produced.
`a, b = b, a + b` updates both at once. Doing it on two lines would use the new `a` when computing `b`.
